\subsection{Mechanisms Read Off the Data}
\label{sec:exp_mechanism}

This subsection adds no new research question. It examines two mechanisms suggested by the fitted scores in \S\ref{sec:exp_prediction}, as well as a data-collection artifact relevant to \S\ref{sec:exp_analysis}.
Figure~\ref{fig:two_futures} and Figure~\ref{fig:mechanism}(a,b) show patterns in the recorded readings, not predictor skill. Their values therefore should not be compared with skill scores. Figure~\ref{fig:mechanism}(c), by contrast, shows the paired skill contrasts reported in Table~\ref{tab:prediction}.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.92\linewidth]{figs/fig_two_futures.pdf}
\caption{One reading is consistent with two opposite next steps. For each task, the next change against the current reading, split by the direction of the step before it; faint marks are transitions and each line is the mean of its group in eight equal-width bins. Transitions whose previous step was flat carry no direction and are dropped, which removes 7\% of transitions on sentiment and up to 66\% on Joint-2.}  % figs/_fig_report.json fig_two_futures n_flat_dropped over n_up+n_down
\label{fig:two_futures}
\end{figure}

At the same reading, the next change differs depending on whether the preceding step moved up or down, across all four tasks (Figure~\ref{fig:two_futures}). The size of this separation does not follow the pattern of memory gains: sentence length has the largest gain in Table~\ref{tab:prediction}, but the smallest separation here. Alongside the results in \S\ref{sec:exp_memory}, this suggests that the window’s benefit comes more from information at the item level than from turn-to-turn trends.
The command plots reveal a data-collection artifact relevant to the caveat in \S\ref{sec:exp_analysis} and Appendix~\ref{app:A7_command_channel}. In both tasks, the applied command remains at the target across the full range of tracking errors in the recorded transitions. These data therefore cannot identify an independent command effect.


\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.92\linewidth]{figs/fig_mechanism.pdf}
\caption{What the command channel carries, and what a learned lifting loses. (a) and (b) Applied command against tracking error, on the two Table~\ref{tab:prediction} tasks that log a per-turn command; color marks the target and repeats the vertical position, which is the point. (c) Paired $\mathrm{Skill}_H$ contrast of the linear case over the learned lifting, on all seven tasks, grouped by the number of attributes a task tracks: a circle marks the five single-attribute tasks, a square Joint-2 and a diamond Joint-3. A filled marker means the 95\% interval excludes zero; the dagger marks a caveated entry.}
\label{fig:mechanism}
\end{figure}
The comparison between the linear case and the learned lifting shows a different pattern. The learned lifting’s skill disadvantage is concentrated in the five single-attribute tasks and is close to zero on Joint-2 and Joint-3 (Figure~\ref{fig:mechanism}c). This pattern does not track the amount of training data: the largest gap occurs in a task fit on 100 trajectories, while the smallest occurs in one fit on 90. Across these seven tasks, the results suggest that a single tracked attribute gives the lifting less structure to capture.

Taken together, the window distinguishes opposite next steps at the same reading, while the skill gap associated with a learned lifting is larger on single-attribute tasks than on multi-attribute tasks.
